utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. I noticed that Mr. Mladic is here as the next witness. For the record, I note that the start of the proceedings for today has been delayed by 15 minutes, upon the request of counsel for Mr. Mladic. Also, for the purpose of the record, I'd like the counsel for Mr. Mladic to introduce himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I'm Branko Lukic, and today I'm here on behalf of Mr. Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Mr. Lukic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we proceed with Mr. Mladic's testimony by way of introduction and background, the Chamber briefly notes the following: The accused in this case, Mr. Karadzic, filed a motion for subpoena for Mr. Mladic on the 18th of April, 2013. On the 5th of July, 2013, the Chamber informed the parties that it would postpone the determination of this motion until such time as the Appeals Chamber issued its decision on the Zdravko Tolimir's appeal of this Chamber's decision compelling Tolimir to testify in this present case. On the 13th of November, 2013, the Appeals Chamber issued its decision with respect to the Tolimir appeal in which it denied Tolimir's appeal and held that the protection against self-incrimination afforded to the Tribunal's accused persons, pursuant to Article 21(4) of the Tribunal's Statute does not preclude the possibility of accused persons being compelled to testify in proceedings which do not involve the determination of the charges against them. On the 11th of December, 2013, the Chamber issued its decision on the subpoena motion, finding that the requirements for the issuance of a subpoena to Mladic had been met and that Mladic's submissions relating to his ill health and his commitments to his own case did not rise to a level that the Chamber should exercise its discretion against issuing the subpoena. On the 23rd of December, 2013, the Chamber denied Mladic's request for certification for leave to appeal the decision to subpoena Mladic and on the 22nd of January, 2014, denied the Prosecution and Mladic motions for reconsideration of this certification decision. Now I turn to Mr. Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, for interrupting you. I know this is not usual.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I informed your staff that I would kindly ask Your Honours to allow me just several minutes to address Your Honours this morning before the testimony of Mr. Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: By all means, Mr. Lukic, yes. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As Your Honour just read, we filed several motions to prevent Mr. Mladic from testifying, and this time I will just briefly try to add several new points and emphasise some of the most important topics. In our view, Mr. Mladic cannot and does not want to testify because of his poor health. Upon the advice of ourselves as counsel, he hereby invokes his right not to testify, due to the unfair prejudice and harm that would be result from said testimony, not only to his health, but to the rights of afforded to him in his own case. We have been told by medical experts, among other things, that he suffers from deception of memory. This is a category of memory disorder, meaning that someone cannot differentiate between the truth and fiction because they are confident they speak the truth even if not doing so. Because of gaps in their memory due to the damage caused by the stroke or other injury, they make up facts to fill up the holes and believe these facts are the truth. We believe this renders Mr. Mladic unfit to testify as a witness. In addition, two Defence medical experts and one of three experts appointed by the Registry have concluded he is at risk of transient ischemic attack if exposed to stress. We believe this, too, makes it inappropriate and harmful for him to be forced to testify. We ask that Mr. Mladic be examined by a team of experts who would determine his medical condition and if he were able to testify. Due to his poor health condition, Mr. Mladic is not able to read and analyse the documents with his attorneys, which is necessary in order to prepare for his testimony. Moreover, he is not able to concentrate and analyse a single document. If we were able to -- if he were able to testify, he would testify in his own case, but because of his poor health, he cannot do that. His indictment, as you know, is almost identical to the indictment of Mr. Karadzic. His trial is still ongoing, and no one can force him to testify at his own trial. Forcing him to testify in this case is the nullification of his right to remain silent. It is our humble position that, by this procedure, the Tribunal violates his basic human rights. And, at the end, I just want to thank you once again for letting me shortly express our views on this topic. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic, for your submission. If the parties would make any observation with regard to the submission of Mr. Lukic. First, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, I believe that you have already ruled on all of these issues that have now been placed before you. And I would note that Dr. Karadzic believes that General Mladic is the one person in the whole world who knows best what happened during the war in Bosnia. And this is Dr. Karadzic's front line right here between the Prosecution and him. And he is asking General Mladic to do his best to help him show the truth of what happened during the war. Because, for Dr. Karadzic, he's -- believes he's fighting not only for his own freedom but for the continuity and existence of the Republika Srpska. And so he realises it's difficult for General Mladic, that General Mladic is not well, but he asks him to do his best and to give the best testimony he can give here today. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. Robinson. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, let me begin by noting that in our submission, Mr. Robinson's position borders on, if not spills over into an inappropriate pitch to a witness that would not in normal circumstances be countenance. I think the Court is aware of the Prosecutor's position on this matter. I think it was expressed fairly clearly in our motion for reconsideration. As Mr. Robinson has noted, these issues have been submitted and ruled upon. I leave it to the Chamber whether or not Mr. Lukic's submissions add anything to the Court's analysis upon which its position earlier rested, but we would otherwise have nothing to add to our earlier submissions with which the Court is thoroughly familiar, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the -- with respect to your points with regard to alleged violation of Mr. Mladic's right, the Chamber is of the view the issue has been sufficiently dealt with in our previous decisions. And with respect to the health issue, while the Chamber notes your submission, but finds that a further independent medical assessment is not required at this stage. In its decision granting the motion to subpoena Mr. Mladic and denying the motion for certification, the Chamber was satisfied that it had sufficient medical information before us in deciding that Mr. Mladic's health concerns didn't rise to a level that would warrant the Chamber exercising its discretion not to grant the subpoena. And there's nothing to suggest that there have been new developments since then which would warrant a further medical assessment. Therefore, we deny the request. But the Chamber, of course, notes that it is amenable to suggestions as to how to organise today's and tomorrow's sitting schedule to address any health concerns Mr. Mladic may have. And we deal with his right as it rises, in particular, his rights pursuant to Rule 90(E) and Article 21. Now I turn to Mr. Mladic. Mr. Mladic, would you kindly rise and make the solemn declaration, please. Mr. Mladic, do you hear me in the language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do, Mr. Kwon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Will you make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kwon, ladies and gentlemen, as for this Hague Tribunal, this Court, I cannot stand it, and I do not recognise it, and I cannot testify before it. I cannot take an oath. Because this is pressure against me as a person, against my health, against my people. These continue to be sanctions, and things have really been brought to an end. I kindly request that you give me the following possibility. With all due respect to President Radovan Karadzic and the efforts that he made and has made for the salvation of our people, and I contributed somewhat to doing some good, I wouldn't want this trial to fail, so I would like to ask you, if you have the possibility and the time, to hear me out. I wrote seven pages last night before Saint Sava's Day. Today is Saint Sava's Day. So if you don't mind, I would like to read that out. And after that, I can take an oath. I do not recognise this Hague Court. It is a NATO creation. It is a Satanic court, not a court of justice, and it is trying us because we are Serbs, because we protect our people from you. It --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic, I'm cutting you off. Please be seated. I will consult my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic, as you know, we have our rules in which our proceedings should proceed. So I would recommend you, again, to take the oath and answer the question, if you will, to the questions posed by Mr. Karadzic. We will not allow you to read out the documents.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I kindly ask that you allow me to read out not a document but my statement that you will be interested in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic, I must let you know that wilful refusal to comply with the terms of subpoena may constitute contempt of the Tribunal which is punishable after the 1st of July, 2013, pursuant to Rule 90 of the Rules of Mechanisms for International Criminal Tribunals by a term of imprisonment not exceeding seven years, a fine not exceeding 50.000 euros, or both. So I will ask you for the last time: Will you take the solemn declaration, Mr. Mladic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kwon, you are considerably younger than I am. You are exerting pressure against me for no reason whatsoever. I'm not afraid of anyone but God. My conscience is clear with regard to all matters. Your subpoenas and your platitudes at the The Hague Tribunal and your false indictments, I don't care one bit about any of that. I don't want to tire these people over there, and all of you. I am going to make this statement but I do not recognise your Court, The Hague Tribunal. It does not exist for me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So I turn to you, Mr. Lukic. It's clear that Mr. Mladic is refusing to testify.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: He is waiting now to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, I am going to testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Don't be nervous, Mr. Kwon. You're from Korea. Bells of alarm are ringing there too. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And could the security people please bring my teeth from the cell so that I could speak better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, the Registry will take care of it. Do you like to have a short adjournment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Apparently seems okay, but it -- I will turn to you as well, Mr. Lukic. And, Mr. Mladic, if it is not possible for you to speak without denture, we'll rise for some time. Because I was told that you left your denture at the Detention Unit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So you like to testify when denture arrives?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. Yes. Because I haven't got any teeth now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, the Chamber is of the view it's better for rise for 15 or 20 minutes in order to understand him better. We'll have a break for 20 minutes and resume at 10.00. --- Break taken at 9.40 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. I now turn to you, Mr. Mladic. Before you commence your evidence, I'm --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not receiving interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you hear me now? Just -- if the usher could assist the witness hearing --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now it's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Now do you hear me well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can hear you, Mr. Kwon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. I will repeat. Before you commence your evidence I must draw your attention to a certain rule of evidence that we have here at the Tribunal; that is, Rule 90(E). As you may know well, under this rule you may object to answering any question from Mr. Karadzic, the Prosecutor, or even from the Judges, if you believe that your answer might incriminate you in a criminal offence. In this context, "incriminate" means saying something that might amount to an admission of guilt for a criminal offence, or saying something that might provide evidence that you might have committed a criminal offence. However, should you think that your answer might incriminate you and as a consequence you refuse to answer the question, I must let you know that the Tribunal has the power to compel you to answer the question. But, in that situation, the Tribunal would ensure that your testimony compelled under such circumstances would not be used in any case that might be laid against you for any offence, save and except the offence of giving false testimony. I take it that you understand that, Mr. Mladic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, Comrade Kwon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Excellencies. Good morning to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, General, sir.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MLADIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, you wanted to say something to the Chamber and the parties to the proceedings. I do not want to deprive you of that opportunity. Can I invite you to state what you wanted to say now as part of your testimony after you have given an oath.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MLADIC
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I will have a word with my colleagues as to -- whether to allow it. Please be seated for the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: As you know well, Mr. Karadzic, this is not an examination in direct --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, this -- this form of a -- allowing the witness to speak at his liberty is not conducive to finding the truth as we ruled in your mode of testimony earlier on. We'll not allow you to ask the witness to read out his statement. Please proceed with your examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have now received a correction in the interpretation because, first, I was told that you would allow it, but I now hear you will not allow it. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, I hope that you will have an opportunity to say what you wanted to say on cross-examination or in response to my questions. Can you tell us what were the positions you held during your military career in the briefest of terms?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MLADIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, Honourable Judges, I'm 71. I held numerous positions throughout my career, from 1965, when I became an officer, until I was arrested by this Court. In response to your question, I can say that I believe that this Court holds records with the exact dates of my various terms of service. I can say that in peacetime, I served in Macedonia, in Skopje, in Kumanovo as battalion commander; as -- in Ohrid as regiment commander; in Stip as the commander of the 39th Infantry Brigade; and on two occasions I served at the command of the 3rd Army, that's to say the 3rd Military District in the operations department. There are records to that effect and I can't recall reliably the dates. In response to your question, with all due respect, I would like to say the following: I cannot and do not wish to testify here because of my health. And I would like to state, upon the advice of my Defence counsel, that I reserve my right not to testify, and I reject -- or I refuse to testify for the reasons that my health may be impaired and as a result of my rights. Mr. President, since Mr. Kwon refused to allow me to read this, I wish to say that I wrote my statement on seven pages. I think it would be interesting. I don't know if the Court will accept this or not, but I would like the opportunity to read this out aloud for the benefit of the audience, the general public, and you, and for the sake of the people. I'm not defending myself. You're not defending yourself. We continue to defend our people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic, I'm cutting you off. You are supposed to answer the question posed by Mr. Karadzic. Mr. Karadzic, please proceed with your next question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, did you ever inform me either orally or in writing that the prisoners from Srebrenica would be, were being, or had been executed?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MLADIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, Radovan, I cannot and do not wish to testify for the reasons of my health. And upon the advice of my Defence counsel, I wish to state that I reserve my right not to testify and I refuse to testify because it may impair my health and because of my rights as an accused in my case. And I have touched upon the events that you are asking me about in this statement that I have written. However, Judge Kwon will not allow me to read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic, I'm cutting you off here again. Mr. Lukic, I take it Mr. Mladic is invoking his right pursuant to Rule 90(E).

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, you are right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I will consult my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: To maybe cut things short - I'm sorry - he will do this after every single question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Exercising its discretion, the Chamber has decided not to compel the witness to answer this question, despite the protection afforded by Rule 90(E), in light of his right against self-incrimination as an accused whose trial is pending before the Tribunal. I ask the accused to proceed with his next question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, the two of us, did we ever come to an agreement or have agreement or understanding that the citizens of Sarajevo would be subjected to terror by shelling and sniping -- or sniping?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MLADIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I cannot and will not testify for the reasons of my health. Upon the advice of my Defence counsel, I wish to state that I reserve my right not to testify and that I refuse to testify because it may impair my health and prejudice my rights as an accused in my own case. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic, do you intend to refuse to answer every questions that are supposed to be put by Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I will give the same answer to every question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, do you wish to put each and every question you suggested?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Excellencies. There's three more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: For the same reason, the Chamber will not compel the witness to answer this question. Mr. Karadzic, please proceed with your next question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, what were the reasons for the shelling or sniping by our army against Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MLADIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I cannot and do not wish to testify for the reasons of my health. Upon the advice of Defence counsel, I wish to state that I reserve my right not to testify and refuse to testify because it may impair my health and prejudice my rights as an accused in my own case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: For the same reason, the Chamber will not compel the witness to answer the question. Yes, proceed, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Excellencies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The fifth question, in that case, is moot so there's only one more question left. General, sir, amongst the two of us, or the leadership in general, was there an agreement or an understanding to expel the Muslims and Croats residing in the Serb-controlled areas?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MLADIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I cannot and do not wish to testify for the reasons of my health. Upon the advice of my Defence counsel, I wish to state that I reserve my right not to testify and that I refuse to testify because it may impair my health and prejudice my rights as an accused in my own case. If allowed, I may read out what I wrote down here. It may prove interesting. And I suggest that I read this out. It's only seven pages. It's not much. And I kindly request the Court to accommodate my request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, Mr. Mladic. Mr. Karadzic, do you have further questions?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Excellencies. I only wish to say that I don't know the contents of this statement, and despite all the risks, I wanted Mr. Mladic to be allowed to read this out. Of course, it is up to the Chamber to rule on this matter. At this point I have no further questions. Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. For the record, we would ask that the statement be received and marked for identification so that there can be some record of what General Mladic wished to say in the event that the issue of the Chamber's failure to compel him is raised at a later date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't see a basis upon which the Chamber should receive his statement. Speaking for myself, I have no difficulty with the Defence receiving his statement on their own and consider what to do with it later on. But I'm not minded to receive on the part of the Chamber. Mr. Tieger, do you have any cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Then that concludes your evidence, Mr. Mladic. Thank you for coming to the courtroom. You may be excused.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for preventing me from stating what I wanted to say. And you have confirmed my thesis that The Hague Tribunal is not a court of a law but a Satanic court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I cut you off, Mr. Mladic. My thanks also go to Mr. Lukic. And I take this opportunity to express the Chamber's thanks to the transportation team from the Dutch police for their hard work and for their dedicated co-operation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll rise before we proceed with the next witness. But I have a couple of matters to deal with before that. Mr. Lukic, you may be excused as well. Thank you again.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: First, the Chamber notes it remains seized of the accused's motion for the transfer, temporary transfer of detained witnesses Dusan Jankovic and Mitar Rasevic in which the accused submits that he had sought to obtain verification from the Bosnian government that the requirements of Rule 90 bis (B) are met with respect to both Jankovic and Rasevic but had not received the response from -- from the government. On 12th of December last year, the Chamber issued an invitation to the government of BiH to co-operate directly with the accused by providing the relevant information. On the 7th of January, 2014, on the basis of correspondence received in the interim, the accused wrote to the government of BiH requesting further information regarding Jankovic. Since that date, no further information has been filed on the record. So -- so, Mr. Robinson, could you please advise the Chamber of the current status of this motion in relation to Mr. Jankovic as well as Mr. Rasevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. President. With respect to Mr. Rasevic, he is no longer in the custody of the authorities of Bosnia and Herzegovina and he will come voluntarily, so we withdraw our request for a transfer order with him. With respect to Mr. Jankovic, we asked the Court to issue an order to transfer him on the dates that we've requested even though we have not had a definitive response from the government. When we wrote to them on the 7th of January, we received no response but it's clear from the public records in Mr. Jankovic's case that he has served -- has been sentenced to 21 years in prison. The sentence is final. And so, therefore, there are no court proceedings scheduled in his case, nor would his testimony in this trial here in 2014 delay his release from that 21-year sentence. We can't do anything more to get the Bosnian government to provide the information. As you know, they normally don't answer us directly but usually require invitations from the Chamber and we -- after they corresponded with us to verify the date of birth of the individual back in the 7th of January, we've heard nothing from them. And we don't believe that a transfer would be timely unless the Chamber issues an order at this time for the transfer. If they have any information, they can object to that order. They've already been served with the original motion, so they're well aware of our request and have never filed any objection so far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: However, the Chamber notes that Rule, in particular Rule 90 bis (B), requires prior verification that the condition set therein have been, indeed, met. So can I hear from you, Mr. Tieger, whether the -- as Mr. Robinson argues in his submission, that this absence of objection by the government of BiH would be sufficient for the purpose of Rule 90 bis (B).

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, it would not seem so on its face as the Court has impliedly noted. However, I'm prepared to meet with Mr. Robinson and evaluate the entire backdrop to the exchange to see if, under these particular circumstances, some implicit acknowledgment can be gleaned from the information provided. But beyond that, I think the Court's point seems to be well taken on the face of the Rule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber will consider this issue. But in the meantime, I would like you to continue to get the verification from the government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll rise for 20 minutes and resume at ten past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would the witness make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vujic. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable. Before you commence your evidence, Mr. Vujic, I must draw your attention to a certain rule that we have here at the international Tribunal; that is, Rule 90(E). Under this rule, you may object to answering any question from Mr. Karadzic, the Prosecutor, or even from the Judges if you believe that your answer might incriminate you in a criminal offence. In this context, "incriminate" means saying something that may amount to an admission of guilt for a criminal offence or saying something that might provide evidence that you might have committed a criminal offence. However, should you think that an answer might incriminate you and as a consequence you refuse to answer the question, I must let you know that the Tribunal has the power to compel you to answer the question. But, in this situation, the Tribunal would ensure that your testimony compelled under such circumstances would not be used in any case that might be laid against you for any offence save and except the offence of giving false testimony. Do you understand that, Mr. Vujic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Vujic.

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let me just ask you to leave a short pause between questions and answers and to speak slowly so that everything can be recorded properly. Have you given a statement to my Defence team?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we show in e-court 1D49061.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On the left-hand side of the screen, can you see the Serbian version of that statement?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you read and signed this statement?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see the last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this your signature?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did this statement faithfully reflect everything you've said to my Defence team?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I were to put to you the same questions today, would your answers be essentially the same as in the statement?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC
utterances.text: Yes, they would.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tender this statement under Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objections, Mr. Zec?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Good morning. No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D4242, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then I will read in English a short summary of Mr. Vujic's statement and then I will have a few questions for him concerning one document and tender that document as well. [In English] Drasko Vujic was mobilised in late 1991 and sent as a member of the 5th Battalion of the 343 JNA Brigade to Slavonia, where he stayed for 45 days. After that, he went back to Prijedor, and when the crisis in Prijedor broke out, he started forming a unit from the Urije area (Prijedor 2) local community. In 1995, he became a member of the SDS and then he became vice-president of the Municipal Board and an assemblyman in the municipal assembly for one term. The unit formed by Mr. Vujic had about 900 to 1200 men, mostly people over the age of 50, many of whom were non-Serbs who joined the unit voluntarily. The unit was engaged in the zone of a small and big road underpass where Prijedor-Centar is separated from Prijedor 2, with the task of patrolling to prevent the movement of unknown people, tension or any incidents. In the morning of 30th of May, 1992, Muslim armed units attacked Mr. Vujic's soldiers from a park located between the two underpasses and from a nearby firm. One of the soldiers was killed in the attack, while the others reacted to the surprise and put up resistance. During the clash, the Muslims fired at an ambulance car that was on his -- its -- his way to town and seriously wounded the driver. After one hour of fighting, the Muslim units were pushed back and withdrew towards the River Sana. This was the last major attack by the Muslim units in the recruitment zone of Prijedor 2. During the fighting, one enemy soldier was captured. He wore a camouflage uniform with a green headband, a Cherokee hair-style, and the Islamic markings of the moon, star and lily. After revealing that Prijedor was attacked by several armed groups from different directions, the prisoner was escorted to the garrison and handed over to the security organs. After this episode, the battalion did not take part in combat operations until September 1992, when most of the battalion was sent to the Gradacac front line, while a small part received the task of mopping out Mount Kurevo, where Muslim units were based. One of the soldiers who took part in the fighting at Kurevo was wounded while one other died. Mr. Vujic was informed by courier about the rebellion of the prisoners at Keraterm but his unit did not take part in the incidents. During the summer of 1992, the battalion's patrols were present in the vicinity of the mosque in Puharska, when the mosque was destroyed in an explosion. Mr. Vujic personally helped the people who had been injured, among whom there was a Muslim man who was put in Mr. Vujic's car and taken to the hospital, where he received medical treatment. The soldiers who were on patrol were severely shocked and some suffered hearing damage. Mr. Vujic did everything he could to reassure the residents of Puharska and to prevent any further attempts at disturbing them. In the summer of 1992, units were sent to search Puharska on the basis of information that many Muslims who were seeking refuge there were suspected of having taken part in the clashes in Kozarac and Hambarine. The Muslim population supported the operation in security, as they were aware that the presence of extremists was a potential threat for them. About 30 men were singled out and transported to Omarska. The other residents remained in their own homes. In 1992, various Serbian paramilitary units roamed around Prijedor municipality, causing great problems to both the Muslim and the Serbian population. Mr. Vujic personally arrested a number of these Suva Rebra unit, one of the paramilitary formations active in the Prijedor area. The paramilitary soldier was disarmed, tied up, and later escorted to the prison in Gradiska. There were several cases when Mr. Vujic co-operated with the Muslim population, helped them, and protected them. The official authorities in Prijedor did not forcibly deport the Muslim population, nor did they have the intention of destroying the Muslim population as a group, wholly, or partially. And now I would have one question for Mr. Vujic within the chief examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vujic, in paragraph 1 of your statement, you say that in your battalion, you had between 900 and 1200 men, mostly people over 50. In our language, we would call them the third category of draftees; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You also say that you had a lot of people of other ethnicities, Muslim, Croats, Roma, and Ukrainians; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D49062 is the document I would now like to show the witness. Sorry, I meant 061 -- no, no. 062 is okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vujic, can you tell us what this list is and who made it?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC
utterances.text: I made this list, preparing for giving evidence today, from the records that I have in my possession about the engagement of soldiers. I singled out the names of people who were non-Serbs and who were members of my unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you read out aloud the first two lines? I mean the title.

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC
utterances.text: List of people of non-Serb ethnicity who are members of the 3rd Motorised Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Here on page 1 we see 41 names. Were all these people non-Serbs, mainly Muslims, Croats, and Ukrainians; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On this page, we see numbers from 42 to 86. Are they also all Croats, Muslims, Ukrainians, Protestants? Which ethnicities and religions are represented here?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is the second page of the list. There are Muslims, Croats, Roma, and Ukrainians mostly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We have a column indicating year of birth. And what is the last column?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC
utterances.text: That's the length of service in the unit for each individual.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So the last date is in 1996 when the unit ceased to exist.

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC
utterances.text: Some were members of the unit from the first day to the last; some left the unit due to various circumstances; some were wounded; some were killed, unfortunately; and others were mobilised for shorter terms and served for a certain period in the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Where were these people from and where did their families hail from?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC
utterances.text: They lived in areas of replenishment of this unit, which means Cirkin Polje, Urije, Puharska, Orlovaca, Orlovci and Garevci, although some people were from other local communities in the Prijedor municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Their families and civilians, where did they live and how were they treated by the authorities of Prijedor municipality?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC
utterances.text: Their families lived in their homes. They continued to work, those who had jobs. Those who were farmers continued to be farmers. They were not intimidated or mistreated in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tendered this document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, this document has one more page. I believe the final number was 133.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Pages 3 and 4.

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is the end of the list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Zec, do you have any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll mark this for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D4243, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And you have no further questions?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I have no further questions in direct examination, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Vujic, as you have noted, your evidence in-chief in this case has been admitted, in its most part in writing; that is, through your written statement in lieu of your oral testimony. Now you will be cross-examined by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor. Yes, Mr. Zec.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Vujic. You told us in your statement that you were member of the 343rd Prijedor Motorised Brigade. You were in Croatia in 1991. You returned to Prijedor and work on military matters. While working on the military matters, Mr. Vujic, you attended meetings with SDS officials; right?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC
utterances.text: Officially I did not attend a single meeting of the SDS at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: This Chamber has received evidence regarding -- regarding a document called Variant A and B. Simo Miskovic testified here that Variant B was implemented in Prijedor; transcript page 45374. The A-and-B document envisaged two stages of preparation. The first stage was related to introducing around-the-clock duties, Crisis Staffs, Serbian Assemblies, methods related to Territorial Defence, and the like. Do you remember, Mr. Vujic, attending a meeting during which these issues were discussed?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 10937B. This is a record of a meeting with Prijedor regional representatives regarding military matters. It is undated but we know from the SDS Municipal Board book of minutes from where this was taken that it is from December 1991. 65 ter -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: You will have it now in front of you, sir -- on the screen in front of you. It starts by noting that 18 members were present. "Simo Miskovic, president of the Prijedor SDS Municipal Board, opened the meeting with a presentation of the instruction which had come from the Assembly of the Serbian People in Bosnia and Herzegovina." It notes that the establishment of a Crisis Staff and the defence secretariat were the purpose of this meeting. There are ten items listed, some of which I already mentioned. Below number ten it says: "The above represents the first stage of preparations ..." Do you remember attending this meeting, Mr. Vujic?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we turn to second-last page in English and last page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: If you look towards the bottom of the page, Mr. Vujic, we see name Drasko Vujic saying that this was too big job to be accomplished with such a tight schedule. So you were present at this meeting; right?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC
utterances.text: I don't remember attending this meeting.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We didn't hear you, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And what is your objection about?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is not a meeting of the SDS, and this does not concern papers A and B. This is about the recommendation of the -- the Assembly of the Serbian People of 10 December. So it's not a SDS meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Zec went through from the first page and then witness was able to read the document, so I don't see any problem with it. So whether he remember having attended this meeting, and he answered in the negative. Shall we continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would tender this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: There's no foundation for it through this witness, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't understand. No foundation?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: The witness isn't able to speak to anything about what happened at this meeting. He isn't able to recognise it as an accurate record or reliable account of what took place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I -- I don't think Defence is challenging the authenticity of this document, are you?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, in the sense that we don't know where it came from. We have no information about the authenticity. But, nevertheless, it may be authentic and it may be admissible through another witness but not through this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Witness is referred to in this document as having made an intervention.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct Mr. President. But I don't believe that makes it admissible, simply because a witness is referred to in a document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Do you like to add anything Mr. Zec?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. President, as you already noted, the document is authentic. It's relevant. It's only question whether the witness remember being there. But there's -- otherwise, there is no -- any obstacle of you admitting it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you intend to put further questions with respect to this document to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. This simply was impeachment point, about the witness being in the area of [indiscernible] on military matters, as he confirms in his statement. But the only point is that he was at this meeting with SDS, which he denied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think your assistance, Mr. Tieger, just be seated. Let me take a look. How do we know this is a SDS meeting, Mr. Zec?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Simo Miskovic presided the meeting, and there is a reference in the document that he is the president of the Main Board. So it was SDS officials, so that's -- and another point, it comes from the book of the SDS Main Board book of minutes. This is only excerpt. So in that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Title of this document reads: Meeting of the representatives of Prijedor municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And I refer to this book of minutes of the SDS Main Board with -- which reflects meetings of the SDS. Now whether -- what -- they referring to what officials, that's -- I agree not absolutely clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: With respect to his attendance in a meeting with some SDS members, I -- the Chamber is of the view we have a basis to admit it. We'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6610, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: In paragraph 6 of your statement, you talk about your proposal to the Muslim TO to hand over their weapons before the clashes and searches, and you say some complied. Mr. Vujic, this Chamber has received evidence that all the weapons and ammunition belonging to the Territorial Defence units had to be stored in the JNA depots even before the period you talk about. It's P3201. And, in fact, Mr. Vujic, the weapons that belonged to the TO units in Prijedor were placed under the command of the 343rd Brigade; right?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC
utterances.text: No, that's not right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 05029.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can you confirm that 343rd Brigade was renamed to 43rd Brigade after the VRS 1st Krajina Corps was established?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC
utterances.text: The exact date of reformulating the name of the brigade is something I'm not aware of. I know that on the 21st of May there was general mobilisation. After that, the brigade was renamed. From the 343rd Brigade Motorised Brigade, it was renamed the 43rd Brigade. Would you allow me to clarify something in relation to that first question. I expected you to ask me why that was not so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Vujic, I will -- we will go through. If you now look on the screen, you will see article from "Kozarski Vjesnik." In the second paragraph in English and second page in the B/C/S, first column, Radmilo Zeljaja says: "Our command with the approval of the corps managed to get together both the weapons and technical equipment from the Territorial Defence units of the municipalities: Prijedor, Sanski Most, Novi Grad, Kozarska Dubica, as well as Cazinska Krajina region and place them under our control in our depots." So, Mr. Vujic, 343rd Brigade took control of the TO weapons; right?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC
utterances.text: At the time that we were talking about a moment ago, that is to say, the time before the attack on Prijedor, and before Puharska, weapons had not been handed over, all weapons, rather, had not been handed over by the reserve Territorial Defence and the reserve police. And it was not placed under the control of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I tender this document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, we -- he has read out the portion that contradicts the witness's testimony and we think that that would be enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Following our practice, I tend to agree with Mr. Robinson. But do you like to add anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I'll move on. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: In paragraph 7, in paragraph 7 of your statement, you say that your battalion did not take part in combat operations until September 1992 when you went to Gradacac except for mopping up at Kurevo mountain. Are you saying, Mr. Vujic, that the unit -- that until September the battalion did not participate in combat activities at front lines involving -- involving two unarmed forces?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC
utterances.text: Yes. But took part in the fighting at Mount Kurevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And the battalion, in fact, was involved in the take-over of the power in Prijedor; right?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC
utterances.text: The battalion did not have any function in relation to the take-over of power in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 25839.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: This is a article from a bulletin of the 43rd Brigade. It says in the middle of the page: "Commander of this battalion, Drasko Vujic, a man who was among the first who felt the fascist vibration of the centuries' old enemies said: The people of Podkozarje know very well how it feels to suffer the war atrocities and the fascist evil deeds. That is why we had to avoid the fate of our grandfathers. We had to be ready for when they come. The old mistakes had to be avoided." When you say, Mr. Vujic, "we had to be ready," you were referring to the preparations in late 1991 that we talked about; right?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: You also say: "That period of activity of a battalion that was still not official on the paper only was characterised by the participation in the taking over of the government from the Muslims." Mr. Vujic, you acknowledged here your participation in the take-over of the power in Prijedor which took place in late April 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC
utterances.text: On that day, when power was taken over, the battalion did not move its units in any way. Except since the preparations for the take-over of government were rather secret, it was only the night before that that I found out there would be a take-over. And my superior command issued me an order - orally, truth to tell - that the units should be prepared at its positions and no order was issued to move the units from these positions. That is why I say that the units had already been organised in part and ready to prevent any kind of surprise that would not work in favour of the citizens of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: But you were clear here in -- in this article. You said "participation in the taking over of the government." You participated. Didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC
utterances.text: I'm going to repeat it once again for you. The battalion did not have any order and there was no move on the part of units at any level. That is to say, it did not take part in the take-over of power. For me take-over of power -- or, rather, participation in take-over of power means, to my mind, to go directly and carry out certain tasks in the territory of the municipality of Prijedor in the territory of the town itself. And in this case, that did not happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And you go on and say: "The defence" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: First of all, could you confirm with the witness whether that's what witness said in the interview?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I also thought that's clear in the interview, but he is explaining in a bit different way so I thought I should [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Where does that inverted comma end?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: As I understand in the article, it says -- from the point when it says, "The command of the brigade said," and there's a column, I -- it's my opinion that's all he's -- what he was saying to the journalist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you confirm having said so, Mr. Vujic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot remember this statement of mine given to the journalist as a whole. As a matter of fact, I don't even remember giving any kind of statement to a journalist at the time. However, this is certainly beautification of the situation on the part of the journalist. That's for sure. And an attempt is being made to leave the impression that there was more power than there actually was, in terms of take-over. I told you a moment ago what the status of my unit was. What the tasks were, and how we carried them out, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue, Mr. Zec.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: You go on and say: "The defence of Prijedor from the Muslim fundamentalists" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Where do we see it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: It's on the same portion. It should be middle of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: "The defence of Prijedor from the Muslim fundamentalists, the participation in the struggle for the liberation of Kozarac."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you see that passage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not see that. I have the page in front of me, but I cannot find my way.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: In B/C/S, it's on -- in the column to the left towards the bottom. Should be the last paragraph in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So now we move to the next page in [overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... in the English, correct. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: "The participation in the struggle for the liberation of Kozarac." And: "Punishment of the Hambarine residents who were the first to spill the blood of the Serb young men." Mr. Vujic, the spilling blood reference relates to the incident of 22nd May, 1992, at the check-point in Hambarine when two Serb soldiers got killed and several wounded; right?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And "punishment of the Hambarine residents" relates to the Serb attack at Hambarine during which the entire area was razed to the ground with many killed and expelled non-Serbs; right?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC
utterances.text: What is meant here is the punishment of perpetrators of crimes that were committed on that day in Hambarine.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I tender this document -- this article, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6611, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: These military operations in Prijedor, Mr. Vujic, took the form of targeting Muslims and Croats by attacking and destroying their towns and places of residence and detaining men; right?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I? Just one objection. In respect of the previous document, and also in the question of Mr. Zec, it is being suggested that it was the inhabitants of Hambarine that were punished, and that is not what the original says. It says --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Vujic answered that point, I think. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Vujic, do I have to repeat my last question or you can -- you can answer?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC
utterances.text: Please repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: The military operations in Prijedor took the form of targeting Muslims and Croats by attacking and destroying the towns and places of residence and detaining many; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC
utterances.text: The objective of the military operation was not to destroy the civilian population or to destroy facilities, property. Rather, to respond through combat to the participation of those who opened fire and killed Serb soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: This Chamber has received evidence regarding the mopping-up operations in Prijedor that the resistance of Croat and Muslim formations was weak followed by mass surrender; that conscripts of Muslim nationality asked to be released from the units for the reasons of massive destruction of their towns; and that the ARK SDS leaders publicly advocated moving and expelling Muslims and Croats. P3662, P3911. These reasons, Mr. Vujic, caused non-Serbs to fear for their lives and leave; right?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC
utterances.text: That is not right. Because the Muslims and Croats had left at their own initiative, considerably earlier. They left all units. Very few of them stayed on. So I have a few examples from that time as to how those few who had stayed on reacted, and those who responded to the call-up to obstruct the JNA and not respond to mobilisation were the main perpetrators of these unfortunate events.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And, at the same time, Serb officials praised members of the 43rd Brigade for their achievements in Prijedor; that's correct?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC
utterances.text: I don't know in which way they praised them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Well, let's have a look.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And, Mr. Vujic, this Chamber also received evidence regarding the commendation of the units engaged in Prijedor, including, Hambarine and Kozarac, by the command of the 1st Krajina Corps saying that they set an example how one should act while defending Serb republic; P3656. Now if you look at the screen in front of you there is an article from "Kozarski Vjesnik" about the celebration of -- or the Vidovda in Prijedor barracks. Among present were members of the 43rd Brigade and 5th Kozara Brigade, their commanders and other officials. At page 2 in English and to the right side in B/C/S, there are text of telegrams sent from Ratko Mladic and Momir Talic. At page 3 in English, and in the box in the middle of the B/C/S page, it says: "The soldiers and superiors of the 43rd Prijedor Motorised Brigade were very happy to hear the news that the president of the state and Supreme Commander, Dr. Radovan Karadzic, has awarded the brigade with the Nemanjic medal for heroic acts in the armed struggle and setting a positive example for acts achieved so far." President also awarded Colonel Arsic. Mr. Vujic, so the fact is that the units involved in Prijedor operations were praised by the highest military and political leadership of Republika Srpska; right?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC
utterances.text: This document shows that the unit was commended and that its commander was promoted. However, the commendation does not refer to fighting where there was no resistance. This was fighting where there was strong resistance. And how. Serb soldiers were being killed. There were casualties on both side. And unfortunately, this was a merciless war. It is for that reason that the unit managed to fulfil its task and, of course, since this is Saint Vitus's Day, it is the time when certain analyses are carried out and commendations are provided to those who contributed to the accomplishment of the mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I tender this article.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we will receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6612, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: You talk -- you talk in your statement about the mosque in Donja Puharska and the way it was destroyed. You say that the explosion was strong which you heard from your home about 1 kilometre away. Mr. Vujic, the mosque was completely destroyed in this explosion; right?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: In order to destroy a building this way, one would need a lot of explosive and preparation; right?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC
utterances.text: I assume so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Despite all the preparation one would need to take, you say that the patrolling units who were there patrolling round the mosque did not see anything at any point of time; right?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: This Chamber has received evidence that dozens of other religious facilities in Prijedor were destroyed the way this mosque was destroyed. And you know this was happening in Prijedor with respect to other non-Serb religious facilities; right?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC
utterances.text: I heard of some later, and I heard of some immediately after the events involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: You say in paragraph 11 that after the mosque in Donja Puharska was blown up, you assured the citizens that you would prevent further disturbing after there was no major incidents. In fact, Mr. Vujic, several days after the mosque was blown up, Djordje Dosen came to Puharska and took Fadil Dizdarevic away. His body was subsequently found in the Sana river; right?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 25837. This is -- this is -- will be a file containing a statement of Rasim Dzafic and several -- several photographs. We need e-court page 4 in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: "Dzafic" --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Could we see the first page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: "Dzafic said" --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: To whom it was given [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: "Several days" --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can you not see it on your own with your e-court?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: No. No, not me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could Registrar approach the bench.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm told that you should be able to see it on your own, with your e-court.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Yes, Excellency, if I give up the transcript. But what is now shown, I can't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, you can see it while listening to the -- to the witnesses and trial attorneys. You can go into your e-court briefly, if necessary. I think the -- that can be done without -- without prejudicing your following the proceedings. Yes, we'll continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Dzafic said: "Several days later, our neighbour Fadil Dizdarevic, came to repair the hodza's house." And then he continues: "The criminal, Djordje Dosen, also known as Djole, found him there. He said he took him to the car and drove off." And then he said: "A day or two later, Fadil's body was found in the Sana river. His chest was riddled with bullets." So, Mr. Vujic, the fact is that non-Serbs were continuing to be targeted after the mosque was blown up; right?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC
utterances.text: You skipped something here that has to do with the destruction of the mosque and my efforts after that. But I know that a certain Djordje Dosen, nicknamed Djole, was a person who created problems both for the Serb and the Muslim population. He was not a member of my unit, and this is the first I hear of this, as of many other cases, many other things that were done by Djole, and are mentioned during this trial, not only today but generally speaking, and that's how I found out what Djole was doing and where he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And we will come back to Djole in a moment. But let's see next page in English. In the -- in the last paragraph, Dzafic says that: "In the course of the same evening, the Prijedor Catholic church was destroyed." Mr. Vujic, did you hear this second explosion when the Catholic church was blown up, after the mosque was blown up?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I heard it. It came about several minutes after the first explosion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Let's see next page in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: This is the mosque in Donja Puharska before it was blown up; right?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we have next page in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And this is after it was blown up; right?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC
utterances.text: Possibly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we now turn the page after the next one in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Do you recognise this as remains of the mosque in Donja Puharska?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC
utterances.text: I cannot claim with certainty that this is exactly what I saw that day. What is possible is that this is what the mosque looked like, that most of it was destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we see photographs -- after next one again, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: This is public -- public utility company from Prijedor called 4 July clearing the remains of the mosque. Do you know when this was? 1992 perhaps?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC
utterances.text: I don't know when this happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we see next photographs in the both -- both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: So this is the house of Rasim Dzafic after the explosion; right?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC
utterances.text: I should think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: This is the house of Zekerijah Kusuran; right?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we have next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Do you recognise this house as described below the photograph?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to tell whose house this is on the basis of the photograph. I can read in the caption that is Muhamed Mirsirlic's house. It stood exactly across from the mosque and I know that it was damaged. And, in fact, the way I see this photograph, it does look like the house that was in the previous photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I tender photographs only.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we hear about the provenance of the photograph, when it was made and by whom? It says September 1992, but where does it come from? Is this part of some investigation documentation?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I refer Mr. Karadzic to the last page of the statement in B/C/S. The witness says who took the photographs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You can tell the accused. I think it's -- it's a fair question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Then we -- can we have last page of the statement that we looked. It should be page 4. Page 4 in -- in e-court.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, now we can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: In English, it's last page of the statement. And the witness says that this was recorded by Mirvan Besic, son of Dzemal, who is currently in the United States. So that's the provenance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Robinson, you have no objections to -- to -- to the admission of photographs only.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President. I think given the witness's comments about them that it's admissible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll admit them.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6613, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Zec.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's go back to Djordje Dosen, also known as Djole, that we talked about.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: He was a member of the Serb forces in Prijedor; right?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC
utterances.text: Djoko Dosen was a member of the 343rd Brigade for several months only in the very beginning. Later on, he was not a member of the brigade anymore, and this was, in part, due to a decision that I made. Since I knew Dosen from before the war, I came across him when he was a member of a unit in Slavonia. He was frightened out of his wits because of the war. He was in shell shock. He was completely unusable, as it were. As I came to Prijedor, I learnt that Djoko Dosen had a smaller unit under his command. The unit executed his orders and tasks. What I didn't know was where these tasks had come from. My conclusion was that he was doing everything on his own initiative, and this proved to be true. Because, at one point, the brigade commander tasked me with taking over the command over the mobilised soldiers on the basis of the territorial principle, including the local commune of Orlovaca, where Djoko came from, Orlovci and Garevci. As a result, my first contact was with Djoko when he responded to my call-up. He came to the headquarters and I told him there that, pursuant to the commander's orders, he was resubordinated to the then-17th [as interpreted] Battalion. I also ask asked him to provide me with a list of troops and inventory of the weapons at his disposal as soon as possible. He refused to do so there and then. He told me that he would not comply with my order. My immediate response was this: For as long as I'm in command of this unit, you, Djoko, will not be in it, not even as a private, let alone any officer. He found it an impossible situation. Several days later, I went to Orlovaca. This was the place where he was active, and he was a native of Orlovaca, and I mean Djoko Dosen, and it was through a great deal of effort that I managed to put together an official unit and appointed a commanding officer. I said that I had a hard time doing it. I had to investigate a great deal of effort because I was met with the resistance on the part of Djoko Dosen and his men. Still, it all ended well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And then are you saying from that point that Djole was subordinated to the units?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC
utterances.text: From that point on, Djole was no longer subordinated to the unit. He wasn't even listed as a member of my unit. He didn't receive any sort of tasks from me. Even if he had received tasks from me, he would not have received them or carried them through.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 46, line 20. It's not much -- it's not of much importance. But for the sake of accuracy, it's not the "17th Battalion," but the "7th Battalion."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you agree, Mr. Vujic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was the 7th Battalion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And, in fact, Mr. Vujic, this Chamber has received evidence that by July 1992, 1st Krajina Corps intelligence and security organ reported that all the groups, these self-acting groups that you are referring to, that all of them were -- they became part of the 343rd Motorised Brigade and were carrying tasks in organised fashion. So, in fact, all these groups, such as Djole, they were under the command of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And this is, Your Honours, P25494.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: So that, in fact, was the situation; right?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC
utterances.text: This was not about the unit. This was only about Djole. Other members of his unit were resubordinated at a later stage and were exemplary soldiers. I only spoke about my dealings with Djoko who was not under anyone's command and whatever he did was at his own initiative.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness said: And they were exemplary soldiers. And this wasn't -- oh, it is now in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I spoke about Djoko only, whereas you use the plural: All those other paramilitaries. And we didn't mention any others. Not yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Shall we take a break now?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll break for 45 minutes and resume at quarter past 1.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.31 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zec, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Vujic, talking about 1995, you know that the unit under Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, also known as Tigers, were deployed to Prijedor, Banja Luka, Sanski Most area in 1995. You know this; right?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC
utterances.text: In certain segments I was aware of Arkan's unit which was present in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And do you know, as this Chamber knows, that Arkan's unit committed crimes in Bosnia in 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with the activities of this unit in Bosnia-Herzegovina. It was only toward the end of the war in 1995 that I had direct dealings with elements of that unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Did you know that in 1995 that Arkan's unit committed crimes against remaining non-Serbs, as this Chamber knows; P3056. Did you know that, in 1995?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC
utterances.text: Which area is that in reference to?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
