utterances.text: Krajina area: Prijedor, Sanski Most, Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC
utterances.text: My activity were always outside of the municipality of Prijedor. I didn't have any contact with Arkan and his members, so I'm not familiar with their participation or deeds.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: With respect to Prijedor, do you know that the remaining non-Serbs were expelled from Prijedor, including, Dr. Ibro Beglerbegovic, who you referred to in paragraph 15. Do you know -- did you know that?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't know when Ibro Beglerbegovic left or whatever happened with him. When it comes to Prijedor, save for 1992 when I knew that he was in his home, and when, on one occasion, and I mentioned this in my statement, I was in a position to help him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And it's already in your statement. But going back to Arkan's unit, your battalion conducted joint operations with police and Arkan's unit in 1995; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC
utterances.text: That was the time when, for the first time, I had certain contacts with Arkan's unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: So they were in your area of responsibility. You were fighting with them, together; right?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC
utterances.text: This was not my area of responsibility. By happenstance, it was dictated by the fighting. My unit happened to be in the defence area of Ostra Luka and Sanski Most, and that was where I found some of Arkan's soldiers. Prior to that point, what I knew of Arkan in Prijedor was in a very ugly context, involving my soldiers. Those who happened to be resting at some point were arrested by Arkan's soldiers, and their heads were clean-shaven. And outside of my approval, they were transferred --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: So then perhaps did you arrest Arkan's soldiers? Did you arrest Arkan for not only committing crimes but also disturbing your soldiers? Did you do that?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC
utterances.text: You didn't allow me to finish my sentence. And I was just about to say that, at the point when I wanted to do, so I was prevented from doing so. I was in a different battle-field. Why is it that you're not interested in hearing me out? Why don't you let me finish? Two or three sentences more won't do any harm. I said that I was in a battle-field. I said that my soldiers who were resting were taken against their will to a different battle-field by Arkan and their heads were clean-shaven, and I was some [as interpreted] kilometres away from the area, and I was not in a position to do anything in relation to these actions by Arkan, and I never met up in person with Arkan.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In line 6, the witness said, "200 to 300 kilometres away," not "some."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Since you didn't take any action against Arkan's Men, did you also know, as this Chamber knows, that it was Mr. Karadzic who sent them there into your area of responsibility? Did you know that? It's P3056.

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC
utterances.text: I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vujic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zec. Do you have any re-examination, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just briefly, Excellencies. Can the witness be shown P2494. It was already cited. P494 -- or, rather, 549. There was an error in the transcript at the time. Yes, that's the document for which the Prosecutor said that it was proof of the fact that this was Dosen's group. Can we have page 2, please. Page 2, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Paragraph 2 from the bottom where it says, "active in the area of Prijedor were ...," can you tell us which were the groups identified in this document?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC
utterances.text: In the area of Prijedor, there were several active self-styled groups, such as Macko's [phoen] group from the village of Micevici [phoen], I believe, led by Stojan Vracar; then Zolje's group led by Sljevcevic [phoen], aka Zolje; and Ciga's group led by Radanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Next page for the English.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Paragraph 3 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC
utterances.text: Should I start from the beginning?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: No need.

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC
utterances.text: Aka Cigo from Omarska. As general mobilisation was carried out, these groups came under the 343rd Motorised Brigade and implemented their tasks in an organised fashion. In the area of Bosanski Novi there was the group of bandits called Suva Rebra.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us is this consistent with your knowledge of these various groups, and, secondly, is there any mention of Dosen's group here?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC
utterances.text: I am aware of the existence of all these groups and their commanding officers. From what I can tell, there is no mention of Dosen here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The Suva Rebra group is that the one you mention in paragraph 14 of your statement, a member of which you arrested?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC
utterances.text: There was only one group active in our area and it was called Suva Rebra. It hailed from the area of Novi Grad, what was then Bosanski Novi.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At page 41, the Prosecutor said that there was a patrol -- a group -- that your group, actually, patrolled around the mosque. Was it indeed the case that it patrolled around the mosque and what was its patrolling area? How large was it?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC
utterances.text: That's what I wanted to explain, that we didn't participate in these events at all. This area has a small river, Puharska, running across it, and on one bank of that river, that was where the mosque was situated. My patrols consisted of two members, senior members of an advanced age, and they were moving on the left-hand side in relation to the mosque. When the explosion took place, they were some 50 metres away from the mosque, that's to say away from the explosion site. As a result, one of them was injured, although both of them were under shock and both were knocked to the ground as a result of the explosion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did I understand this correctly, that outside of your patrolling area and outside of the area where there was the mosque, a small river ran?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: At page 32, it was suggested that the weapons held by the Territorial Defence were relocated to the JNA barracks. Do you know how successfully this measure was, indeed, implemented? Or to what extent it was not successful, in terms of having all those who were authorised to have weapon, such as companies, TO depots, et cetera, to have them turn the weapons over?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC
utterances.text: All those who had weapons kept them. In the various companies, they did not get organised into units but they did at the level of the local commune. One such TO unit which consisted mainly of Muslims, talking about Puharska, kept the entire weaponry of the TO. A reserve police force was attached to them under that same principle. As a result, I decided that in that area - that is to say, Puharska - I should not be deploying my units. I believed that their presence would be a source of irritation for the local population residing in the area, and I was apprehensive of the fact that we may even cause a conflict there. My intention was to try and reach an agreement in order to disarm these units which, at that point, were, in fact, paramilitary, to avert any fighting and harm coming to the civilian population. I was partly successful in that, because there were some individuals there who understood what my intentions were and supported them, so they implemented this idea in part. The only request on their part was that no lists should be drawn up of the individuals surrendering weapons. I asked them to go through the disarming process themselves because I was afraid that my presence there and the presence of my soldiers there would have negative effect. Seven or eight individuals were actively participating in this process of partial disarming, and I emphasise partial because Puharska had close to 5.000 inhabitants. All the weapons that they agreed to surrendering in this way could fit into a tractor trailer. Those who gathered these weapons - and I'm still grateful to them for that - handed these weapons over to the barracks. It is quite certain that the great majority of them did not hand their weapons over because most of the weapons that were surrendered were civilian hunting weapons and only a couple of them were semi-automatic and automatic military rifles. There were among them those who deliberately obstructed this process and even went as far as to physically abuse the individuals who decided to hand their weapons over. So the action was partially carried out, and I was quite happy with that because I was able to continue engaging in human, private and professional, and any other sort of communication with these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And my last question: What became of the individual who surrendered their weapons and co-operated with you with a view to maintaining the peace? And I'm referring to the Croats and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC
utterances.text: I continued to co-operate with them, and, as I've said in my statement, they trusted me. So, on several occasions when I helped them, and at their request supplied them with some medication that was very difficult to get hold of, especially at that time, including antibiotics and medicine for heart diseases, and whenever they asked me I supplied whatever I could without any money given in return, because, I, as a commander, could take this medication from our military infirmary. And, anyway, we co-operated in every possible way until the attack on Prijedor and that area causing casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What was the doctrine of the JNA in terms of co-operation between the army and the people, when you mentioned these medicines?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC
utterances.text: I explained on my personal example how that happened in my area, but I also had the full support of my superior command, and I didn't need to conceal from my command whom I was helping, including the cases of -- when I supplied food to some families who were in need.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How long did this co-operation last; and how long did they stay in their homes?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO VUJIC
utterances.text: The co-operation lasted till the very end, considering that a large number of them remained in their homes until the end of the war. But what happened after the attack on Prijedor, considering that some of the units that had attacked Prijedor withdrew through Puharska and, as far as my unit is concerned, they had free passage there. That's why they used this route to attack. That attack actually resulted in what I initially thought was the number of 30 people, although I later learned that it was perhaps closer to 60 people being taken away on two buses. And among them were some people who would certainly not have been taken away if I had had any influence in the selection because they had proven their goodwill and readiness to have everything done peacefully and in the best possible way.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Mr. Vujic, that concludes your evidence. On behalf of the Chamber, I would like to thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was told that we need some five minutes for preparation for the next witness, but before we do so, I have another couple of matters to deal with. First, we will -- the Chamber will issue an oral ruling on the Prosecution motion to exclude, in part, the evidence of Witness KW426 filed on 24th of January, 2014, and on the Prosecution request for leave to reply to Karadzic's response thereto filed on the 27th of January, 2014. The Prosecution requests that the Chamber order that paragraphs 14 to 33 be excluded from KW426's statement on the basis that they detail events in Kotor Varos, a municipality that has been dropped from the indictment, and are therefore irrelevant to the charges against the accused. The accused responded on the 27th of January, 2014, opposing the motion and submitting that the expected evidence is relevant to rebut the evidence of Prosecution Witness Dorothea Hanson, that Kotor Varos was representative of how nation policies were implemented in the municipalities. At the outset, the Chamber notes that the witness statement does not indicate that the witness has any knowledge as to the implementation of national policies in the municipalities. In fact, in relation to Kotor Varos, he states that as far as he recalls, he attended only one meeting of the Crisis Staff there. Kotor Varos is one of the municipalities which have been removed from the indictment. While the Chamber has heard some Prosecution and Defence evidence on this municipality from a number of witnesses, either in passing or in some more detail, the portions of witness's statement relating to Kotor Varos are very detailed and do not relate to -- do not relate to the charges in the indictment or to a determination of the accused's responsibility. The Chamber further notes that the accused was given ample opportunity to cross-examine Ms. Hanson on all of her reports and that during the course of his cross-examination, that the Chamber admitted a large number of documents he put to Hanson on the topics she addressed in her reports. The Chamber, therefore, grants the motion and concludes paragraphs 14 to 33, allows the accused to tender the remainder of Witness KW426's statement pursuant to Rule 92 ter, and denies the Prosecution's request for leave to reply. For the next matter, shall we upload Exhibit D4204? This is the statement we received as 92 ter statement of Defence's 207th witness, Radomir Radinkovic. Next page, both in English and B/C/S, page 2, just related to question 1. In the process of reviewing this statement, the Chamber noticed that the term "concentration camp" was used in the draft English translation of the statement under question 1, which in B/C/S reads "sabirni logor." However, having looked at the B/C/S version of the statement, the Chamber is concerned that the reference "concentration camp" may be the result of an incorrect English translation. Thus, the Chamber will order the CLSS to revise the draft translation of this exhibit, focussing specifically on the question -- answer to question number 1, on page 2 of the statement, and report back to the Chamber by the end of this week. We will rise for five minutes. --- Break taken at 1.47 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, would the witness make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable. utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And before you commence your evidence, Mr. Witness, I must draw your attention to a certain rule of evidence that we have here at the international Tribunal; that is, Rule 90(E). Under this rule, you may object to answering any question from Mr. Karadzic, the Prosecutor, or even from the Judges, if you believe that your answer might incriminate you in a criminal offence. In this context, "incriminate" means saying something that amount to an admission of guilt for a criminal offence or saying something that might provide evidence that you might have committed a criminal offence. However, should you think that an answer might incriminate you and as a consequence you refuse to answer the question, I must let you know that the Tribunal has the power to compel you to answer the question. But, in that situation, the Tribunal would ensure that your testimony compelled under such circumstances would not be used in any case that might be laid against you for any case, save and except the offence of giving false testimony. Do you understand that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will now read out in English a short summary of this witness's statement. [In English] Witness KW609 was a resident of Prijedor municipality. The witness worked at the Omarska camp from May until August 1992. He states that security at the camp was provided by members of the public security service of Prijedor and its Omarska department. The Omarska camp commander was Mr. Zeljko Mejakic, commander of the Omarska branch of the SJB Prijedor. Mejakic's primary duties were to secure the buildings with detainees, provide food and medical care, in co-operation with relevant services. Mr. Mejakic's duty -- deputy, Mr. Miroslav Kvocka, was fired for having taken three Muslims (his wife's brothers) out of the camp. The Witness KW609 states Mladjo Radic was the shift commander at the camp and Drago Prcac was also at the camp. The Witness KW609, all the time it's 609, states that only active police officers had full uniforms. Reserve policemen's uniforms were often incomplete due to the lack of uniforms. KW609 witness states that after the order from Ratko Mladic on the 3rd of August, 1992, the camp was prepared, cleaned, and extra beds put in place for the visit of the International Red Cross on the 4th of August, 1992. Mr. Mejakic was obliged to report to Simo Drljaca and the operational team, part of the latter was also KW609. Simo Drljaca was at the camp twice. Rajko Mijic - Branko Mijic, probably - who conducted interviews with detainees at the camp communicated with Drljaca over the telephone every morning about everything that happened on the previous day as well as providing Drljaca with the list of people to be brought in for an interview. KW609 states that there was "support unit" from Banja Luka of approximately ten people (size of a squad) under the command of Commander Strazivuk, present in Omarska. They arrived with a blue APC and according to words from Mejakic, they were taking gold and other valuables from detainees that came to Omarska. This act made tensions between the support unit and policemen under Mejakic's control. The support unit left these events, were communicated to Simo Drljaca. There was second-ring security outside Omarska camp under military security detail. Military officers under control of Lieutenant-Colonel Majstorovic initially also carried out operative processing of mainly individuals who were members of the Yugoslav army. There were ten mixed teams working from Omarska. There were ten State Security Service inspectors. Similarly, public security service had ten inspectors who were under the command of Ranko Mijic. There were also members of military security under the command of Lieutenant Majstorovic. Such organisation/separation of work was defined by Mr. Simo Drljaca in one of his orders. Furthermore, analysis of documents was done jointly and persons of security interest would then be further processed. Dusan Jankovic was Simo Drljaca's chief deputy and responsible for the co-ordination of the implementation of an order to collaborate with Banja Luka Security Services Centre. The municipal authorities in Prijedor were providing Omarska with food, while Prijedor Medical Centre provided medical services. It was requested that any individual taken to remand centre must be accompanied with proper documents showing the reasons for detention and/or custody. This was only respected at the beginning. Interrogations were conducted on the first floor of the two-storey buildings. Initially people were interrogated on the basis of area they came from and then categorised in three groups: Group 3 had no information of security interest; group 1 were ring-leaders of hostile activities; and group 2 were supporters of hostile activities. First- and second-category detainees would be transferred to Manjaca, while third-category detainees would go to Trnopolje. Transfers happened at the end of July or beginning of August 1992. During the whole period, around 3.000 people were interrogated. KW609 was aware of only one case of physical force being used to obtain information from a detainee during the interrogations. Each inspector had to write an Official Note after each interrogation. After further statements from individuals mentioned in the Official Note were taken, criminal reports were created. KW609 was only aware of one case of a detainee being brought for interrogation with fresh bruises. In July 1992, KW609 was notified of an event where 18 detainees have been killed upon the recommendation and the list compiled with the Inspector Rade Knezevic. KW609 reported this incident to Mr. Simo Drljaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Before I finish my direct examination, Witness, do you have a back problem? And could we perhaps ask the Trial Chamber to grant us additional breaks, if you need them, if your back hurts.

utterances.speaker: KW609
utterances.text: For the time being, I don't have particular problems. If something happens, I will ask the Chamber to assist me.

utterances.text: By all means, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have one remark to make. I heard in the interpretation that I stated something concerning a detachment instead of a squad. utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it should be squad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Just a second. Refer -- coming back to the issue of Official Note, suppose they are third-party statement, when confirmed and commented upon by the witness, there's a basis to be admitted. Do you agree, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.text: Well, I recall, Mr. President, that -- that -- well, first of all, that would not be the case, as I understand it. Of course, if it fell within the lex specialis of 92 bis. utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But when we talk about lex specialis, refer to the statement that have been produced for the purpose of current proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That -- correct. As I recall and, again, I'd have to review the research we undertook on that. Certainly that would embrace -- I mean, that was an issue at one time. I think it became expanded over time, that at one time it was seen to be simply statements taken only intended to be submitted as statements and then it was broadened to some extent. So I wouldn't want to speak specifically to that. But I -- I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My point is this: So instead of waiting until tomorrow and before the cross-examination starts, it would be better for Mr. Karadzic to deal with these Official Note live with this witness, if he is minded to tender these Official Notes at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We're not minded to tendered those Official Notes unless you felt it was an indispensable part of the testimony that was being admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. That being the case, I will invite Ms. Sutherland to begin her cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, sorry, Mr. President, should have caught your point earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: KW609
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: When you testified which is now the basis of your evidence in this case, you were shown a document, and in our case it's 65 ter number 25594, it's a cover letter of the Prijedor municipal secretariat regarding reimbursement of the cost of using buses for the needs of the Crisis Staff in July 1992. Do you recall that document? Do you recall seeing that document when you -- when you testified?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's an associated exhibit but I don't know the exhibit number. That's why I referred to it by the 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It's now Exhibit D4247, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At this moment, I cannot recall a document discussing money and collection of payment. I would need to see the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can you see it on the screen in front of you? It's asking for the amount of 273.000 dinars for the cost of transport for the month of July. You said in relation to that document when discussing this document that detainees were transported in -- in Autotransport bus from Keraterm to Omarska, and you also said that this transfer took place two or three days after you started working at the Keraterm camp. So this would have been late May 1992, yes?

utterances.speaker: KW609
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You also testified that once a number of people from Prijedor municipality were brought to Omarska during the day. You recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: KW609
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If I could have 65 ter 18905, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, what will be coming up onto the screen is a table setting out Autotransport Prijedor buses used in 1990 -- for -- in July 1992 for the use of the Crisis Staff, the police, and the army. Now, if we look at the entry for the 9th of July, 1992, we can see that passenger transport was used to transfer detainees from Keraterm to Omarska. Do you recall seeing or hearing of detainees being transferred from Keraterm to Omarska in early July?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we ask for the number under which -- oh, it's the 9th of July. It says -- where does it say that it concerns prisoners, detainees? It would be of assistance.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I can see, these are local lines in Prijedor municipality: Tukovi-Trnopolje, Trnopolje-Banja Luka, Trnopolje-Modrica, Trnopolje-Pasinac, Trnopolje-Pejici. Those were local transport services that operate normally every day in the municipality. Pejici, for instance, is an exclusively Serbian village. I did state that the buses of the transport company Prijedor were involved in the transport of people from Keraterm to Omarska. That's what I said in my evidence at Stanisic and Zupljanin and I stand by this statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I take Mr. Karadzic's point. I did say we can see on the entry for the 9th of July passenger transport used to transport detainees from Keraterm to Omarska. And that wasn't what I meant to say. Looking at the entry for the 9th the July we can see that buses are used, at least four buses for the army's purposes, to go from Keraterm to Omarska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If necessary, we can collapse the English and zoom in to the B/C/S further.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you for that suggestion, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you -- my question is: Do you recall seeing or hearing of detainees coming from Keraterm to Omarska in early July, a large number, four buses?

utterances.speaker: KW609
utterances.text: Yes. Some of the prisoners on whom we had some security information were to be transferred from Keraterm to Omarska. So those persons about whom some security information existed were brought to Omarska for further processing.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And if we could turn the page to page 2 of the B/C/S and also page 2 of the English, we can see the entry for the 22nd of July, 1992, and it shows ten buses for the use of the army going from Prijedor to Omarska and on to Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you recall a large number of people --

utterances.speaker: KW609
utterances.text: I remember that some four buses were returned to Trnopolje from Omarska because we were not able to receive so many people in Omarska. There was not enough room for them, quite simply. Yes, that one case happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I seek to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Two pages.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: It's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Three. It's three in the English -- sorry, three in the English and two in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could identify the dates. 9th of July.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's a two-page document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Oh, yes. We'll admit that. No objection, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6614, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Oh, sorry, if we -- if we just go to page 3 of the English and the second page of the -- of the B/C/S, we can see down the bottom of the list for the Crisis Staff the figure 31, and then the kilometres and the figure of 273.000, which correlates with the other document, the first document, that I brought up which was 65 ter 25594. Your Honour, at this point, the majority, if not all of my cross-examination is going to have to be in private session because of what I'm -- the details I'm going to get into. So I'm terrible sorry for the public that is sitting in the gallery, but there's nothing that we can do about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber will go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If we're moving in -- I have one point I wanted to raise in open session at the risk of being tiresome but I wanted to -- so we don't have confusion. The Trial Chamber asked me a few moments ago whether or not the -- if it is a third-party statement, if it could be admitted, the witness commented on it. The wanted to draw the Court's attention to a ruling in the -- during the (redacted) (redacted) where I think the -- the practice that I referred to earlier was followed in which the objection was made that such document fell within the lex specialis and was considered by the Trial Chamber to -- to be such. And the -- the -- the document was not -- excuse me, was not admitted on that basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But I think we admitted yesterday or the day after -- before yesterday --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Right. That's the reason I went and did the research. Because it -- it -- it struck me at that point that we had shifted from a practice that had been established before, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think there was a confusion what -- as to the scope of the documents produced for the purpose of criminal proceedings. Whether it is limited to the current the proceedings or it includes the proceedings in the former Yugoslavia as well. But I think it has been resolved. We'll come back to that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. In any event, I wanted the Court to have the benefit of the citation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, could the Chamber go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we are now in open session again. Mr. Witness, we continue tomorrow at 9.00. I like to advise you not to discuss with anybody else about your testimony while you are giving evidence here at the Tribunal. Do you understand that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 29th day of January, 2014, at 9.00 a.m. 25
